segments.text: South Korea charged shoppers for thin plastic bags in 1999 to cut waste, only to watch manufacturers
switch to thicker reusable film that escaped the fee and raised handling costs.
In the autumn of 1999, South Korean shoppers began paying a small fee at checkout for
the flimsy plastic bags that had once been handed out without charge.
Policy makers expected the price signal to shrink the stream of single use film heading
to landfills and streets. Instead, bag manufacturers began selling thicker, heavier sacks marketed
as reusable, and those sacks still ended up in the trash after a single trip. Only now,
they weighed more and jammed the equipment meant to sort them.
The fee had been calibrated to the transaction itself, yet the physical film crossed an invisible
thickness line that removed it from regulation while leaving the disposal habit untouched.
What looked like a straightforward conservation measure therefore preserved the original volume
of material sent downstream, only in a denser form that raised new handling expenses at
every sorting station.
This is unintended consequences, episode 121.
The fee emerged from a straightforward desire to reduce the volume of plastic entering municipal
waste streams.
At the time, South Korea was expanding its recycling infrastructure and looking for simple economic
tools that could complement new collection programs.
Officials reason that even a modest charge would make consumers pause before accepting
an extra bag, lowering both litter and the tonnage scent to disposal sites.
The approach drew on the broader international conversation about market-based environmental
instruments that had gained traction in the 1990s.
No one at the drafting stage anticipated that the physical properties of the bag itself
health would become the variable manufacturer's would optimize around the fee.
The policy therefore targeted the transaction, not the material intensity of the product.
Decision makers could see that thin bags were cheap to produce and easy to discard, so
attaching a price at the point of sale seemed the most direct way to interrupt that flow
without banning the item outright.
They worked from the information then available, visible litter, growing landfill pressure,
and evidence from other countries that small charges could shift consumer behavior at the margin.
The charge took effect nationwide in 1999 and applied to thin single use bags at supermarkets and
other retail outlets. Early reports noted a visible drop in the number of bags distributed, which
supporters cited as evidence that the price incentive was working. Retail chains posted signs
reminding customers to bring their own carriers, and some municipalities paired the fee with
public education campaigns. A few industry voices cautioned that the rule defined the regulated
product by thickness rather than by actual reuse behavior, yet those objections remained
marginal during the rollout. Collection data in the first year or two appeared consistent with
the policy's goals, reinforcing the sense that the measure was on track. Proponents could point to
fewer bags crossing checkout counters as proof that the economic signal was being received.
And the absence of immediate complaints about thicker substitutes kept the focus on the
reduction in bag counts rather than on the weight of material still moving through the
system.
Manufacturers quickly introduced bags made from heavier gauge film that exceeded the
thickness threshold and therefore fell outside the fee.
These new sacks were sold as durable, multi-use items, yet most households continued to treat
them as disposable. Because each bag now contained more plastic, the total tonnage of film entering
the waste stream did not fall, and in some streams may have risen. At sorting facilities,
the thicker material proved harder to process. The added stiffness and weight caused jams and
conveyor systems and shredders designed for lighter film. Municipal crews spent extra labor hours
clearing equipment, raising operating costs without a corresponding reduction in material throughput.
it. Consumers, facing a higher per bag price, often bought the thicker version in smaller
quantities, but still discarded it after one use, preserving the original disposal pattern.
The substitution effect thus neutralized the intended conservation outcome, while shifting
the burden downstream to the collection and sorting infrastructure. Over time, the heavier
bags also altered the composition of residual waste, complicating later attempts to measure
progress against landfill diversion targets.
One can trace the arithmetic directly.
If a thin bag weighed roughly 6 grams and a replacement weighed 12 grams, then even a
30% drop in bag numbers could leave the same or greater plastic mass in the waste stream.
The policy had no mechanism to register that the remaining bags carried twice the material,
so the headline success metric of fewer bags masked the unchanged or increased plastic
tonnage.
Facility operators later described the thicker film catching on rollers and tearing screens
that had been calibrated for lighter stock, turning a once-routine maintenance task into
repeated shutdowns.
The causal chain runs from a thickness-based exemption through a profitable product redesign
to an unchanged consumer habit and, finally, to higher operational friction at every subsequent
stage of waste handling.
Once the pattern of substitution became clear, regulators began exploring adjustments to the thickness
definition and to the scope of the charge. Some localities experimented with fees based on bag weight
or with deposit return systems that would reward actual reuse. The original policy was never fully
repealed. Instead, it was gradually supplemented by broader single-use plastic restrictions in later years.
Today, South Korea continues to refine its plastic reduction toolkit, incorporating lessons
about how narrowly drawn price signals can be gained by changes in product design.
Later measures therefore tended to combine fees with explicit material or reuse standards
so that the same substitution path would be closed in advance.
Incentive structures always find their loopholes when the rule hinges on a single measurable
attribute rather than on the underlying behavior.
Here, complex systems resist simple interventions because actors respond to the letter of the
constraint, not necessarily its spirit.
When designing any fee or tax, it helps to model the most profitable substitution path
available to producers and users before the rule is locked in.
How might today's carbon pricing proposals or single use item levies change if manufacturers
are already preparing the next slightly altered product that slips the definition?
